proxy_language: Proto-Indo-European (late, as a conventional stand-in) — explicitly NOT the Creswellian language
proxy_rationale: The Creswellian (c. 14,500-12,800 BP; Creswell Crags, Gough's Cave, Kendrick's Cave; backed-blade industry of the Late Magdalenian/Epigravettian sphere in Britain) left no linguistic evidence. Its language is wholly unknown and almost certainly belonged to a family long extinct, since Paleolithic Britain was repopulated after the Last Glacial Maximum from a southwestern European refuge (Magdalenian/Villabruna-cluster ancestry) and Indo-European arrived only millennia later (Bronze Age). No proto-language can be linked to them. Pragmatic fallback for a naming engine: use a reconstructed PIE-style phonology as a neutral, internally consistent, pronounceable stand-in, or alternatively the Vasconic/Basque-like pattern sometimes invoked for Western European hunter-gatherers (also unproven). This answer adopts reconstructed PIE-style roots for hunting/landscape/animal vocabulary because the roots are well documented, while flagging that no Creswellian speaker spoke PIE. Names should be understood as invented-but-plausible, not real Creswellian.
phonology: Reconstructed PIE (Fortson/Beekes-style, 3-laryngeal): stops *p *t *k *kʷ (*ḱ), voiced *b *d *g *gʷ, aspirated *bʰ *dʰ *gʰ; fricative *s; sonorants *m *n *l *r *y *w; laryngeals *h1 *h2 *h3; vowels *e *o *a (rare) with long variants; vocalic sonorants *r̥ *l̥ *m̥ *n̥. For a simplified game rendering, drop laryngeals to plain vowels/h and aspirates to plain stops or stop+h.
phonotactics: Roots are typically CeC(C) with e-grade vowel (e.g. *dʰeh1-, *h2ner-, *ḱwon-). Syllable shapes (C)(C)V(C)(C); onset clusters of s+stop and stop+liquid/sonorant allowed (str-, pl-, kr-, tw-); no vowel-initial roots in the simplified rendering except with h. Codas are sonorants, s, or stops. Words end in a stem vowel, sonorant, s, or m (nominative -s, accusative -m). Stress/ablaut (e/o/zero grade) alters vowel but is not spelled beyond the e/o alternation.
orthography: Simplified Latin transliteration of PIE reconstruction notation: plain letters p t k g b d s m n l r w y h a e o i u; use 'kw' for *kʷ, 'gh/dh/bh' for aspirates, 'h' for any laryngeal; omit asterisk and diacritics in names (macrons optional for long vowels); no c, q, x, z, f, v, j.
morphology: Inflecting, root-and-suffix. Nouns: root + thematic vowel (-o-/-e-) + case ending (nom. -s, acc. -m, gen. -os/-es/-so, loc. -i, instr. -bʰi); genders masc/fem/neut (fem often -eh2 > -a). Verbs: root + tense/aspect suffixes. Derivation by suffixes: -ent-/-nt- participle/agent, -tor- agent noun, -men-/-mn̥ result noun, -ti- action noun, -ilo-/-lo- diminutive/tool, -eh2 collective/feminine, -yo- adjective/belonging. Reduplication in intensive and present stems (e.g. *dʰe-dʰeh1-).
compounding: PIE compounds are head-final: modifier + head, linked by a thematic -o- (e.g. *wl̥kʷo-, name-style compounds like *h2ner-ḱlewes). 'X of Y' is best rendered as a genitive: Y-gen + X (or Y-yo- adjective + X). Agent names: object + agentive (*deh3-tor- 'giver'; 'Y-maker' = Y-o-dʰeh1-s 'Y-doer'). Names of two-element bahuvrihi type (e.g. 'Red-Antler') = adjective-o + noun.
noun_phrase_order: Adjective before noun and agreeing in case/number/gender; genitive before head noun (Possessor-gen Head), though postposed forms exist; demonstratives precede noun. In simple names: Modifier + Head.

sources: Mallory & Adams, Encyclopedia of Indo-European Culture (1997)

Jacobs et al., 'Late Pleistocene human genome suggests a local origin for the first farmers of central Anatolia' / Fu et al., 'The genetic history of Ice Age Europe', Nature (2016) for population background
Jacobi, 'Creswellian' and the British Late Upper Palaeolithic (Cheddar/Gough's Cave publications, 1990s)
notes: The Creswellian language is unrecorded and unrecoverable; PIE is used only as a conventional, internally consistent stand-in and PIE itself postdates this culture by roughly 8,000-10,000 years. Treat all names as invented. Because Creswellian is not Goidelic, no generated name may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word.
